title: Queen against rook I: the Philidor position
summary: The position where the rook has to leave its king, and the fork that punishes every escape.
part.philidor.title: The Philidor position
part.philidor.summary: The position the whole endgame heads for, and why the move decides everything.
part.fork.title: The fork that punishes the escape
part.fork.summary: A rook that runs far away loses its defender and falls to a check that hits both pieces.
part.ladder.title: The ladder of checks
part.ladder.summary: When one check cannot reach the rook, the queen chains checks until the fork.
part.triangle.title: Passing the move: the triangle
part.triangle.summary: With us to move in the Philidor position, the queen loses a tempo and hands the move back to Black.
part.traps.title: Traps and summary
part.traps.summary: The two mistakes that let the rook escape, and the rules to take to your games.
step.t_philidor: This is the most important position in queen against rook. Black to move. Before I explain, work it out yourself: what moves does Black have, and what happens after each one?
step.t_philidor.hint1: Start with the black king. Count the squares it could go to and see who guards each one.
step.t_philidor.hint2: Now the rook. For each square near the king, ask who captures it there. And if it runs far away, who defends it?
step.intro: Philidor studied this position in 1777. Black king on the edge, rook glued to it, our king on c6, a knight's jump away, and the queen on a5. The black king only has c8, and from there the rook cannot hold (Qa6 attacks b7 again): a7 and a8 belong to the queen, c7 to our king. With Black to move, the rook is forced to move.
step.near: Near its king the rook has no square. On a7, the queen mates on d8. On c7 or d7, the rook falls. On b6, b5 or b4, the king or the queen takes it. Two ways out remain: the king goes to c8, where the rook cannot hold (Qa6 attacks b7 again), or the rook runs far away.
step.pin: Let's take the first way out. The king went to c8 and left the rook with only the king as defender. Attack the rook so that it cannot leave b7.
step.pin.hint: Look for a square on the a-file from which the queen sees b7 and the king behind it.
step.pin.done: Pinned: if the rook leaves b7, its own king is in check. That is why the king could not save it.
step.t_fork: The rook ran to g7, far from its king. White to move. Think: who defends the rook there? Is there a move that attacks the king and the rook at the same time?
step.t_fork.hint1: Nobody defends the rook on g7. Look for a check that, from the same square, also looks at g7.
step.t_fork.hint2: A central square does it: from there the queen sees one diagonal to b8 and another to g7.
step.far: These are the escapes far away, the marked squares. Far from its king the rook has no defender, and an undefended piece falls to a fork: check to the king and an attack on the rook in one move. The rule fits in one line: the first check is almost always on e5.
step.d_fork: Watch how the queen punishes the rook on g7. I play both sides; notice where each check comes from.
step.d_fork.m1: Queen to e5, with check. From there she sees two diagonals: one reaches the king on b8, the other the rook on g7.
step.d_fork.m2: The king escapes the check to a7. The rook is still on the other side of the board, with no one to defend it.
step.d_fork.m3: And the queen takes the rook, still with check, along the seventh rank. Without the rook, what is left is the king and queen mate you already know.
step.efile: Now you. The rook went to e7, and here the check on e5 fails: the rook takes the queen. Find another check that attacks king and rook.
step.efile.hint: Look on the b-file for a square that is also on a diagonal of e7.
step.efile.done: That's it: with the rook on the e-file, the check is on b4. It is the only exception to the e5 rule.
step.t_ladder: The rook is on h7, as far as it can go along the rank. White to move. From here the check on e5 does not hit the rook. How can the queen reach a square that gives check and attacks h7?
step.t_ladder.hint1: One check is not enough. Think of two or three checks in a row, never giving the black king a break.
step.t_ladder.hint2: A long diagonal ends on h7. The checks must drive the king until the queen can land on that diagonal with check.
step.d_ladder: Now the ladder. Notice that the queen gives check on every move until she takes the rook: the black king never has time to help it.
step.d_ladder.m1: First, the usual check on e5.
step.d_ladder.m2: The king hides in the corner.
step.d_ladder.m3: The queen drops to the a1 corner and checks along the a-file.
step.d_ladder.m4: The king goes back to b8.
step.d_ladder.m5: Check on b1, along the b-file. And look at the diagonal: from b1 it runs straight to h7.
step.d_ladder.m6: The king steps out of check, but the rook is in the queen's sights.
step.d_ladder.m7: The queen takes the rook. Three checks and a fork: that is the ladder.
step.d_rf7: With the rook on f7 the ladder is different, this time along the e-file.
step.d_rf7.m3: The queen drops to e3 and checks along the diagonal that reaches a7.
step.d_rf7.m4: The king goes back to the corner.
step.d_rf7.m5: Now the queen climbs to e8: check along the back rank and, in the same move, an attack on the rook on f7.
step.d_rf7.m6: The king steps out of check.
step.d_rf7.m7: And the rook falls, with check.
step.rb1: Your turn, against the most stubborn defence: the rook on b1, as far away as possible. It takes four checks. The path is e5, d4, the h8 corner and, last, the square from which the queen attacks king and rook.
step.rb1.hint: After the h8 corner, the check is on the square next to it. From there, a diagonal reaches b1.
step.rb1.done: Four checks and the rook is gone. That is the longest line of the Philidor position.
step.t_triangle: The same Philidor position, but now it is our move. Any move seems to spoil everything. Think: how can you give Black exactly this position back, with Black to move?
step.t_triangle.hint1: You need nothing new, just the same position with the move switched. The queen can do it on her own.
step.t_triangle.hint2: Use checks, so the black king has no time for anything. Three queen moves are enough, and she ends where she started.
step.white: This is zugzwang in reverse: the position is great, but it is our move. The way out is to lose a tempo. The queen walks a triangle, e5, a1 and back to a5, with two checks on the way, and the position comes back the same, with Black to move.
step.d_triangle: Watch the triangle. I play; notice that the queen ends on the same square where she started.
step.d_triangle.m2: The king goes to the corner.
step.d_triangle.m3: Check along the a-file, from the a1 corner.
step.d_triangle.m4: The king goes back to b8.
step.d_triangle.m5: And the queen returns to a5. The same position, and now Black is to move: the zugzwang is theirs.
step.triangle: Now you make the triangle and pass the move to Black.
step.triangle.hint: Three queen moves: e5 with check, the a1 corner with check, and back to a5.
step.triangle.done: Done: the same position, with Black to move. This triangle turns up throughout the queen against rook endgame.
step.squeeze: Beware of squeezing. Here the queen went to a6 and the king to b6, and the rook checks on c6. If the king takes, the black king is stalemated; if the queen takes, the same. If the king runs, the checks go on. A draw. A queen glued to a cornered king smells of stalemate.
step.false: Now the false Philidor. It looks the same, but our king is on a6, not c6. The rook gains d7, far from our king, and c7 goes unguarded. It still wins, but takes more than twice as many moves. The right king stands on c6, a knight's jump away.
step.recap: To take away: one, Philidor is king on c6, queen on a5, black king and rook on the edge; with Black to move, the rook falls. Two, if it is our move, the triangle e5, a1, a5. Three, a loose rook falls to checks until the fork, starting on e5, except with the rook on the e-file.
step.finish: Now against the machine, which defends well. It is the Philidor position with you to move: pass the move, see where the rook runs and find the fork. After winning the rook, give the king and queen mate.
ex.e01: White to move. It is the Philidor position, but it is your move. What is the first move?
ex.e01.hint: You need to hand back the same position with Black to move. Start the triangle.
ex.e01.solution: Qe5+ (Qd5 makes the same triangle the other way round). Then the queen goes to the corner with check and returns to a5: the position is the same and Black is to move.
ex.e02: White to move. The rook ran to b2. Win it in two moves.
ex.e02.hint: The first check of the rule. From there the long diagonal reaches b2.
ex.e02.solution: Qe5+ and, wherever the king goes, Qxb2. The queen on e5 checks and attacks the rook along the diagonal.
ex.e03: White to move. The rook is on e7. Which check wins the rook?
ex.e03.hint: On e5 the queen would be captured. Look for the check on the b-file.
ex.e03.solution: Qb4+. The queen checks on the b-file and attacks e7 along the diagonal. Qd8+ also wins the rook, along the back rank.
ex.e04: White to move. The black king stepped out to c8 and the rook stayed on b7. How do you win?
ex.e04.hint: The rook has a single defender, and it stands behind the rook.
ex.e04.solution: Qa6. The rook is pinned against the king and cannot move; next move the queen takes on b7.
ex.e06: White to move. The rook went to h7. Three checks win the rook.
ex.e06.hint: The ladder: e5, the corner a1, and the square from which a diagonal reaches h7.
ex.e06.solution: Qe5+, Qa1+ and Qb1+. From b1 the queen checks and attacks h7 along the diagonal: a fork.
ex.e08: White to move. You squeezed too hard with the queen and the rook gave check. Where does the king go?
ex.e08.hint: On b6 the king seems to stay close, but look at the rook check on c6 and count the black king's squares.
ex.e08.solution: Kd6 (or Kd5, or Kb5). On b6, the rook would check on c6 and any capture would stalemate the black king. Away from the rook the win is still there, only longer.
ex.e09: White to move. The rook went to b3. Find the series of checks that wins it.
ex.e09.hint: Start on e5. The final square is g8: from there the queen looks at b3.
ex.e09.solution: Qe5+, Qg7+, Qg8+ and the rook falls on b3. The queen climbs the kingside to the g8-b3 diagonal.
ex.e10: White to move. The most stubborn defence: rook on b1. Four checks, and the last one attacks the rook.
ex.e10.hint: e5, d4, the corner h8 and the square next to it. The diagonal that matters is the one ending on b1.
ex.e10.solution: Qe5+, Qd4+, Qh8+ and Qh7+. From h7 the queen checks along the rank and attacks b1 along the diagonal. It is the longest line of the Philidor position.
key.black: The Philidor position (1777) with Black to move: zugzwang. The king can only go to c8, and from there the rook cannot hold: Qa6 attacks b7 again. The rook, wherever it goes, falls. Diagram from Wikipedia.
key.white: The same position with White to move: the queen draws the triangle e5, a1, a5 and hands the move back.
key.corner: Philidor in the other corner, as in NM BXMSChess's Lichess study. The endgame can finish in any of the four corners.
key.draw: The trap for those who squeeze too hard: the rook checks on c6 and any capture is stalemate. A draw. Wikipedia quotes it from Averbakh.
history: Philidor analysed this position in 1777, and for two centuries the queen against rook endgame was thought to be simple. In December 1978 Ken Thompson, of Bell Labs, finished the first complete database of the endgame and challenged grandmaster Walter Browne to win with the queen in fifty moves against the computer Belle. Browne bet a hundred dollars, said half an hour would be enough, and failed. He studied, asked for a rematch and won the rook on exactly the fiftieth move. Since then the endgame has been taken seriously: Svidler, at the 2001 World Championship, let Gelfand escape by the fifty-move rule, and Morozevich, in Pamplona in 2006, fell into a stalemate against Jakovenko. With perfect play the rook falls in at most 31 moves.
practice: Now against the clock, or without it. The position is almost Philidor's: you only need to put the pieces in place and pass the move. The rest you already know.
